utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To enable us to continue the debate with which we concluded yesterday's session, we will now go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Following our deliberations, the Trial Chamber have decided to hear a limited amount of evidence by posing questions themselves to a witness in closed session, and then we'll make a final decision on the application made by the Prosecution. That hearing will be later in the day. Meanwhile, the evidence of Mr. Vasiljevic will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vasiljevic. The cross-examination by Mr. Ivetic will now continue. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vasiljevic. I'd like to finish up a few points about the operative sweep groups, which you've mentioned at various times in your testimony, including at paragraph 30. Now, you testify in very general terms how a security operative from Djakovica told you about alleged mass expulsions and robberies committed by the OPGs. First of all, is this the same operative covering Djakovica, Pristina, and Mitrovica, because your statement at this paragraph covers all three municipalities. Is it the same operative, or are we talking of multiple persons?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same operative.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you take measures personally to verify, double-check, or further investigate these claims from your operative, (redacted), apart from speaking with him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My job was not to verify the data from the field but to receive reports and briefings from security officers. At the concluding meeting held at the security department of the Pristina Corps, the corps chief of security provided data on the activities of the groups, which tallied with what had been said to me by (redacted) Therefore, I didn't try to verify any data; there was no need and no time for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just the previous paragraph, paragraph 29 of your statement, you clarify that only certain members of the OPG units were linked to these crimes, I suspect rather than the whole units. Do you have any details such as who the specific members were that committed these -- any specific crimes?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know them by their names. It wasn't the way it was put to me during the briefing as to who was in the groups. What they -- what was said was there was a group by the name of Legija, and I already mentioned who was their superior; then the Kosovska Mitrovica cases were mentioned, the one from the Muslim cemetery where they took away a child and they asked for a ransom of 3.000 German marks; then another one at the flea market where bric-a-brac is sold. They came there, fired a few bursts in the air, and the stand owners fled; and that's when they took away the merchandise that was there. This was along the lines of information he put to me. He learned that along the way, and it wasn't the type of information that I was supposed to verify or run checks or investigations on. This was not within my purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So these are the details that you -- that you had. And can I take it from that - and I believe you did testify that you did not recognise any of the enumerated acts or victims from the indictment - can I take from that, therefore, that you have no hard evidence or specific evidence to link either the OPGs or this group you've called Legija or Magla to any of the crimes set forth in the indictment in this case?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't draft the indictment, and I didn't -- couldn't decide what would be included in it. I, in fact, didn't read it in its entirety. I'm just talking about the sections that I knew about and that I was asked about. What for would I actually go into all this?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, am I correct that as far as these allegations that you've made here under oath as to what was reported to you about crimes committed by these groups, am I correct that you actually have no idea whether any of these were investigated or prosecuted by the relevant authorities?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can't really say that I don't have any idea. That is not an appropriate thing to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but that might have been an error in translation. I actually asked -- I did not intend it in that type of manner. I thank you for your response. Now, with respect to these crimes that were reported to you by your operative, do you know whether your operative personally eye-witnessed these crimes as they occurred or was he operating on second- or third-hand information?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I assume that those were -- this was the operational intelligence that he gathered. He seemed rather convincing as he said that, but I think he was not on the site. But he did have reliable operational sources in the field who relayed this information to him. But as far as the bodies on the bus station are concerned, I think there were about 20 corpses there and he knows about it quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right, sir, before we return to that I just have to clear one thing up for you. At page 8, line 15, in response to the question that I asked you whether you had any idea whether any of the crimes were investigated or prosecuted by the authorities, I thought I heard you say in Serbian -- well, you said that you can't really say that I don't have any idea. I thought I heard you say, "I don't know." Is that accurate that you don't know whether any of the events were investigated? Because it has not entered into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's what I thought I heard you say, so I thank you again for that. Now, you mentioned the bodies at the bus station. Do you know whether your security organ (redacted), whether he informed his commander(redacted), regarding the bodies at the bus station?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I assume that he should have informed him, but that was probably a rather notorious fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did (redacted) say that Kovacevic formed a group, Legija, and that Djakovica had a separate OPG? Are we talking about two separate groups?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We were talking about the OPGs and then we started talking about this group Legija in Djakovica. Was it the --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was it the information that you received from your operative that these were two distinct groups; that is to say, in Djakovica that there was in group Legija as well as an operative sweep group?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that was the case because he spoke about the activities of the operational sweep groups in Mitrovica; and as far as Djakovica was concerned, he was talking about the Legija group that he had formed that consisted of 15 members. And my conclusion was that this was not an OPG, because an OPG should have been -- should have included much more people.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, was this Legija then some sort of private armed band?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was not the usual term. You could say that this was some kind of paramilitary unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How is it that (redacted) was able to speak about three municipalities at once, Mitrovica, Djakovica, and I believe also Pristina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not about Pristina. This unit was deployed in the field in a larger area. I had information as to where all the groups were deployed, the military groups. So a battalion would cover a front that would be about 35 kilometres wide and 7 kilometres deep. And three military territorial detachments as part of the operational tactical group would cover a front line that would be 105 kilometres wide and 30 kilometres deep. So because of the nature of the terrain, they covered a lot of ground and they -- he had sources that would come to him to Djakovica from the field and, he didn't even have to leave Djakovica at all if he received this through his operational channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, I recall you testified that you had no way of receiving information from Suva Reka because you did not have an operative in Suva Reka itself. That's a little bit confusing in light of what you've just told us and in light of the fact that according to my information, you did not have a security operative in Podujevo either but you did receive information from Podujevo. Would you agree with me that just because you do not have an operative in a particular municipality, does not preclude the possibility of obtaining information from that municipality; that is to say, the operative need not be based in a particular location to have knowledge of that location?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it is not correct that I did not have an operative in Podujevo. When I got to Kosovo, we first visited Podujevo. The commander of the unit was there and the security officer was there, and I got introduced to them. So there was an operative in Podujevo. Second, all those questions that you're asking now, I am duty-bound to explain that I did not go to Kosovo to check what the MUP was doing. I went there to receive reports from the security organs in the counter-intelligence work, and in addition I received reports about the events in the field. So this is the intelligence that they gathered in the course of their work, but they did not specifically seek that information. As far as Suva Reka was concerned, I mentioned that there was a military territorial detachment in Musitiste. As far as I know, it is in the area of Suva Reka and I mentioned the Albanian that they had said. So I spoke only about the areas that I received reports about from them. I was not some kind sort of a supervisory commission, a part of a commission as we know had proposed to be established. I received information from the security organs, and I simply am now relaying the information that I got from them to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of the 37th Brigade of the VJ was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would now have to think. I did not really communicate with him, so I can't give you his name off the cuff. I know the security organ there. It was Major Bojkovic, B.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, getting back to these crimes you say the OPGs committed, I take it from your information that it can be concluded that these crimes were undertaken by individuals in their personal capacities and were not ordered as a part of a plan on the part of the RJB; that is to say, you did not have information that these crimes were committed or planned by the organs of the public security service of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are two questions in there. The first one's inappropriate; the second part may be okay. So the question for you, Mr. Vasiljevic, is whether you have specific information that these crimes were planned by organs of the public security service.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to clear up -- I have three questions relating to the meetings in May before we move to the June meeting where I'll also have some questions. First of all, regarding the meeting that took place on the 16th of May, between various officers of the VJ. At that meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you proceed, we're finished -- we've completed a section of your evidence at this stage, have we, of your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will go into private session briefly to consider an issue affecting the security of an individual.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The matter discussed will be the subject of consideration by parties. Meanwhile, the evidence so far this morning will not be published until the parties have made their submissions about it in relation to the matter I've raised with them. Please carry on now, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, if we can focus for a moment on the meeting that occurred on May the 16th between various individuals from the VJ. At that meeting, did General Pavkovic talk about "asanacija terena" or "asanacija bojista," clearing of the terrain or the battle-field?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he actually did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did General Pavkovic, at the meeting on May the 17th with Mr. Milosevic, make any complaints that the MUP was either not participating in asanacija, or was only doing it on part of the territory?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have my notes as to what actually was said in the meeting in the debate when he said about problems in the cooperation with MUP; and in his introductory presentation, I think he spoke about the problem, who was in charge of the sanitization or clean-up, and that this depended on who was actually conducting activities in certain parts of the area, so who was in charge of the sanitization. So there was an accusation levied against the military that day conducted -- that they had conducted the activities and that now they had to conduct also the sanitization. I don't know the exact word, but that was the gist of the debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I've one more question dealing with this meeting, and it relates to paragraph 62 of your statement. Can you please explain for me your word choice in the statement in describing the allegation of bodies between the VJ and the MUP. For the VJ, you say 271 bodies of people who "died" in areas covered by the VJ, but then you say 326 people were "killed" in territory where the MUP was active. Am I correct that with respect to both groups of bodies there were, as I think you testified earlier, there were various causes of death such that it would have been proper to say that the people had died in both areas, rather than putting the bias "killed" on the group that were on the territory that you say is under the jurisdiction of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you are right that two terms are being used. Died, that could be from natural causes. I think that the best term would be casualties, and those people died in various circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for clearing that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In relation to both instances, VJ and MUP, are you referring to violent deaths?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Basically, it would be violent death, that would not be death caused by some kind of illness. But as to the actual cause of death, whether these people died as a result of fire from any of the sides or whether these people were executed, we're talking about 326 bodies on one side and 271 bodies on the other side. They were killed in all kinds of activities, so there were individual executions, some were killed in artillery fire, some by NATO air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to move to the meeting that you termed as being the Joint Command that you attended in Pristina in June of 1999. I have some questions on that topic. First of all, in the signed, sworn statement that you have provided us at paragraph 81 of that statement, you claim that General Lukic began the meeting with a briefing and a short report about the presence of MUP forces and their activities before the army generals began their briefing. Now, the prior, albeit draft, and unsigned statements that we received from the Prosecutor for you listed that MUP General Djordjevic was actually the one who gave this report and Lukic was not mentioned at all; then the next draft that we received for you listed General Lazarevic as having made this report. Is it your sworn testimony that you are absolutely positive that this paragraph is correct and that Sreten Lukic opened the meeting of this so-called Joint Command by presenting a briefing on behalf of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm absolutely positive, first of all, that I had never said that General Lukic opened the meeting. I said that he held the first briefing, that he was the first person to take part in the debate. And his rank was not such that he would be the presiding -- the chairperson of that meeting. It was actually Mr. Sainovic who opened the meeting. He made a few introductory remarks, and that's why we had to wait for him. We had to wait for him so that we could start the meeting. So he did not chair the meeting, he did not open the meeting, he did not conclude the meeting, but he was the first to take part in the debate. And had Djordjevic and Stevanovic made any interventions, I would have noted that down in my notebook. I don't have any such notes in my notebook. The first thing that I have is General Lukic, then the commander of the Pristina Corps, very briefly and I made a couple of brief notes; then General Pavkovic; and, finally, Mr. Sainovic made a few brief closing remarks. This is the truth, this is what is contained in my notebook, and I don't think that I used the phrasing that he opened the meeting. I said that he held the first briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that 4D180 -- excuse me, 6D170 be placed on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is the transcript disclosed by the Office of the Prosecutor of your interview with them, specifically the interview conducted on the 23rd of November, 2001. And this is the -- I've extracted from the interview some short quotations therefrom, and I'd like to direct your attention to the first part which we're not getting on e-court. Maybe I'll just read it and then hopefully the e-court will catch up with us. At lines 23 to 25 of page 51 of the transcript, which I believe should be the first page in e-court, when talking about this meeting in June that you attended and asked about who the speakers were, here's what you said then in 2001, sir: "Pavkovic spoke first about the events of the day in the field as far as the Yugoslav Army was concerned, but this was just in Kosovo, not it the whole of Yugoslavia." Sir, this quotation from your transcript doesn't seem to comport with your testimony here today about who spoke first at the meeting, does it, who gave the first report?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said today is true. In 2001, in fact in both situations, I did not take part in those conversations, interviews with the notebook, and I did not know what the interview would be about. And this was based on my recollection at the time. Two years had passed since the events; and when I was in fact preparing for the statement, this is not on the basis of the statement. These are the interviews that I gave when I had the status of a suspect. I did not sign any statements. It is quite possible that I did state this at the time, but at that time I did not really focus on this and I did not have my notebook with me at the time. So what I said here in court today is the positive truth, and I think that it doesn't really matter who took part in the debate first and who was the second person to take part.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony then that Sreten Lukic was the second person to take part in the meeting and give a briefing on behalf MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was the first and the only person that I have listed in my notebook as taking part in the discussion at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I would ask for the second page of this exhibit to be placed on e-court, which is page 52 of the actual transcript. And, sir, at lines 5 to 11, you state to the Office of the Prosecutor: "Then General Djordjevic from MUP spoke about the activities of the day from his side, where -- in other words, where MUP had been commencing the terrain also in terms of losses, people who were wounded, and then he mentioned a place which I don't remember which it was. He said that there was a group located there and that they needed to be dealt with tomorrow, and they would block off this terrain with MUP units and carry this out." Now, Mr. Vasiljevic, you would agree with me, would you not, that for the past six years or so you have consistently stated that General Djordjevic was the one who presented the report on behalf of the MUP at this meeting; and for the first time the other week before coming here to testify -- before starting your testimony here, you for the first time insert General Lukic as the man who gave the report for the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the characterisation. That question says, "you consistently maintained for the past six years." Six years ago he made a statement at an interview where it was said to come up for the first time and he didn't have the notebook. It's not as though he's been repeating it every day for six years.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He testified in Milosevic, and we have an unsigned statement from 2005 [sic] that also had Djordjevic. It's been consistently for the past six years until to 2007, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's three examples, Mr. Hannis. Do you accept the characterisation of the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could have references to those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can gladly upload the unsigned statement that was tendered to us by the Office of the Prosecutor on I believe it was January the 4th, 2007. I could put that into the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's be clear. Mr. Hannis, are you saying that that was not in the unsigned same time?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that was in a draft, that was before this witness had reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, if that's what he was talking about. But I thought he was also talking about prior to testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He was talking about testimony in the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what I am asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That I would have to double check on the reference for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what I want a reference for, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If the problems is the six years, I can take that out. I mean, I can ask the question without reference to that. I think my point is rather clear in any event, and I would just ask for the witness to explain how it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's what I'll do then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, how do you explain the fact that General Lukic is not mentioned as the person who chaired -- who gave a report on behalf of the MUP at this meeting, when your testimony -- your statements during your interview are rather clear and rather full of details as to who presented this report on behalf of the MUP? How do you explain that change in your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I think that you misunderstood -- you said that I testified in 2005 or that I made a statement in 2005. I don't understand English, but I see that 2005 is referred to. In 2001, I made my own statement which I did not even sign or verify. It was recorded publicly, and that is what you said just now. I've explained that; that at that time I did not use a notebook. I was a suspect suspected of taking part in the enterprise in Croatia. So I had been called in for Croatia, and then the conversation was expanded so as to include Kosovo, so I wasn't even prepared for that. I repeat once again, when I was preparing for this testimony, this statement, I had an opportunity to look at my notebook and I said what I said. If I made a mistake in 2001 as to who said it, I claim now what I have in my notebook, that the first person to speak was General Lukic, then Lazarevic, then Pavkovic, and finally Mr. Sainovic. Mr. Djordjevic just mentioned who was absent from the meeting and why. That's the only thing there. I didn't even write that down in particular. So I really don't know what is controversial now when I say under oath that he was the first person to take part in the discussion. I did not use the expression "opened the meeting." I did not use that expression at all and I don't think it's contained in my statement either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's forget that, that's not an issue, opening the meeting; that's a distraction from what this is all about. Mr. Ivetic, is there, in addition to the interview, a statement given by the witness in 2001?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, we -- the first statement we received is from 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's only the interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, the procedure of the Tribunal would normally require you to receive a copy of the recording of your interview in 2001. Did you receive such a copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I got this recording. When the conversation was over, I signed and verified that those were the cassettes concerned. I got the cassettes themselves later. As for the verified statement made then, I never received that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're saying that in addition to being interviewed by the Prosecution, you also gave a statement, which would not be as a suspect but as a witness? Or was there only the one occasion that you were required to give information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was giving information in the capacity of a suspect, and at that time I was not given any statement to verify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, but you were given a recording -- a copy of the recording of that interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which you could verify if you wanted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I had time to check it but I didn't check it. There was no need for me to check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Second question I have is in the trial of Milosevic, did you there say that the MUP report was given by Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly. Maybe I put it that way because I gave a statement here when I came to The Hague and then, again, I did not have the notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2002 before actually giving evidence in the Milosevic trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 2003 I made a statement that I signed to Mr. Nice, because the trial began in 2003 in the month of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the impression I'm getting from the Defence side of the trial is that they haven't seen that statement. Does such a statement exist, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know of a statement. I know there were proofing notes, because they were referred to by Mr. Nice during the testimony they're referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness is saying he signed something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which would undoubtedly make it into a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of a signed document, Your Honour. I'll do some checking during the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The one in 2005, Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 2006, Your Honour. Sorry, that was a mistake. 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The unsigned version in 2006, what was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was a draft that was furnished to the Defence before it was reviewed and signed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A draft of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: A draft of his signed statement that had been presented as evidence in this because, Your Honour, we were running close for the time for him to appear. I sent the draft based on my conversations with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that must have post-dated the 27th of October?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that was between the 27th of October and the 7th of January, when it was finalised. It was a draft of what he had told us in October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivetic, do you have the transcript pages for the trial of Milosevic in which this is referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know from memory that reference is made to Djordjevic or are you unsure?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The only thing I know from memory is that there is no reference to Lukic. Whether he actually was asked to testify about this or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think you have a basis then for putting any other point to the witness other than the one that you've just put, so we can perhaps move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree. I would just ask that if there is a -- any kind of signed statement from 2002 or 2003 that that should be provided to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've already heard that from Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can move to the next topic, resubordination of the MUP. Sir, first of all, I would ask for Exhibit P985 on the screen. Sir, relative to the Law on Subordination, would you agree with me that in Article 17 Law on Defence, which should be on e-court shortly, merely foresees the resubordination of the MUP to VJ forces but only for the carrying out of combat activities and not permanently in all aspects of life?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think Article 17 is on the screen for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We've found the Milosevic transcript where he indeed testified that General Djordjevic gave the statement on the MUP. It's page 15971 of the Milosevic beginning at line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's take this one thing at a time. Do you want to go back to that first of all?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So let's have the Milosevic transcript page on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We can't get it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can read it into the record, that's all I can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Listen to this extract, please, Mr. Vasiljevic. It's an extract from your evidence in the trial of Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, at the stated page in Milosevic in response to a question from the Prosecutor your answer at line 12 starts: "Yes. This was a brief routine report as to what had been going on over the past 24 hours. First, General Lazarevic gave some brief observations regarding NATO operations and then General Djordjevic from the MUP spoke about MUP operations. There was nothing special going on there that I would remember. It all ended with a brief summary as to what should be done during the following day. For the most part, the general from the MUP said that during the course of the next day, the terrain should be cleaned in the area of Drenica, so that was briefly that particular meeting."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's your response, Mr. Vasiljevic, to that evidence you gave in Milosevic, which seems to be inconsistent with what you're saying here? Bearing in mind that you were on oath in that trial as you are in this one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Basically, what was being discussed. I didn't present any other facts. It said the general from the MUP said such and such a thing. No reference was even made to what it was that Djordjevic said. I repeat. I looked at my notebook. Djordjevic said why a person was absent and he -- rather, General Lukic made a report about the situation of the terrain in Kosovo, and he was effectively in charge of the units in Kosovo. If I can provide a free interpretation, it is the commanders who are taking part in the discussion and the reporting, the commander of the MUP forces and the commander of the units of the Army of Yugoslavia. Again, I'm saying that this is just something that was just marginally stated at the time; and as for any disagreement as to what Lukic said or what Obren Djordjevic said, the truth -- the whole truth is this, and I even have expanded knowledge in respect to these few sentences that I said then. Now that I saw my notebook, as I was preparing for my testimony here and now, I did not make any false statements. Perhaps there were some imprecisions as to what person said what, but from here you can see that I did not mention Pavkovic taking part in the discussion; whereas, objectively speaking, he did take part in the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think I asked you about the notebook the other day. I can't remember what the evidence was. Do you have it with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, not right here, of course, but I could get it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can return to Article 17 of the Law on Defence. My question for you, sir, had been: Relative to this article, that it foresees the resubordination of the MUP to the VJ forces only for the carrying out of combat activities or to offer armed resistance and does not apply to other aspects of life. Is that correct? Is that your understanding of that law?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, sir, now, that is to say that resubordination, apart from combat, does not cover all MUP personnel and all MUP activities, such that the VJ does not take over operation of police stations or subordinate the Minister of the Interior, as you implied the other day. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not saying that the Minister of the Interior is being resubordinated. I am saying that within the Supreme Command Staff, there could be a respective of the MUP or the Minister of the Interior; like a general was sent from the Ministry of Defence in order to coordinate at that level. As for the letter that was sent by General Pavkovic that was shown here, it seems to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Before you continue on, would you answer my question because that's my next question. Would you answer my question --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- that in fact the Law on Resubordination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your question's been answered. I was not saying is that the Minister of the Interior is resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about other activities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've already had that answer in relation to his general understanding of the meaning of Article 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to the letter you talked about, Exhibit P1459, a report purporting to be from General Pavkovic to the General Staff complaining about problems with resubordination. This is a document you said lacked a proper stamp evidencing its receipt by the recipient. I take it since you testified you saw it for the first time here, you were not given that report or made aware of it during your trip to Kosovo, which occurred after the date of that report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After what date?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: May the 25th I believe is the date on that document, and I believe your travels to Kosovo were in June of 1999. At the time of your trip to Kosovo, you did not have this report and you were not made aware of it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, likewise, am I correct that at the time you went to Kosovo you did not have and were not made aware of any similar report issued by the commander of the Pristina Corps, General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for General Lazarevic, I did not have any individual contacts with him while I was in Kosovo. I only met him at the meeting on the 1st of June when I came to the command, and he was there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I take it then you did not have any such report or know of any such reports issued by General Lazarevic at the time that you went to Kosovo in June of 1999. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of reports he sent. I did not have insight into his reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to ask you specifically. Am I correct that the first time that you learned of complaints of resubordination by Pavkovic relating to the MUP was after the war in Kosovo was completed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I first heard of that problem from General Pavkovic at that preparatory meeting on the 16th of May when he reported to General Ojdanic. I think that later he only spelled that out in official terms in the document of the 25th of May; that is to say, nine days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, resubordinated MUP units operating under VJ command would still wear standard MUP uniforms and utilise MUP equipment, would they not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During the course of the crisis in Kosovo in 1999, your security organs in the field, they never reported to you of any significant problems relating to resubordination of the MUP, did they?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No reference was made to resubordination problems. It was mutual cooperation that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to be clear, when you're talking about the preparatory meeting on May the 16th, 1999, we're not asking about any complaints about the MUP trying to pass responsibility on to the VJ; we're talking specifically about complaints that the MUP was utterly refusing to resubordinate itself. Is -- was that specific complaint made?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the complaint was made that at check-points, where the military police is, they pass there. Their vehicles and their members pass by ignoring these check-points; and, generally speaking, there is a problem in coordination and cooperation with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was the specific word or word phrase "problems with resubordination" used? Was resubordination a specific topic that was discussed in terms of complaints?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That also has been answered, Mr. Ivetic. "No reference was made to resubordination problems." Could you have a clearer answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, that was with respect to his security organs. I'm talking about the meeting on May 16th, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you need to have the question repeated, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's arguably, but that's been answered as well today, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You were told that that's where it was raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But then he started talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Ask this question. I want to draw your attention to the fact that your 20 minutes are now approaching an hour, but let's try and get this focused, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will try, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was the specific term "resubordination" listed as a complaint made at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was said that the resubordination order had not been observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, moving on to another topic. During the course of your official travel in Kosovo-Metohija, you did not obtain any information whatsoever from your security organs and contacts about activities to clandestinely remove bodies from Kosovo-Metohija and transport them elsewhere in Serbia, did you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was no such information from the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did your security organs on the territory of Kosovo-Metohija, did they report to the organs of the MUP in Kosovo-Metohija their complaints or allegations of crimes? Did they exchange information at all with the MUP organs in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume they did. I did not express interest in that as to that whether they sent any information and to what extent. However, at the level of the security administration and the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia and the state security at that level, we were preparing that and they were discussing that. How many pieces of information we had sent to the republic state security and to the MUP. And what did we receive from them? Nothing. That was the topic of one of our meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have just two areas left; a total of ten questions. But the next portion would need to be in private session, as it relates to part of his statement that was redacted from the public for reasons that the witness stated relating to security?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go into private session for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, the final area, sir. Yesterday you -- when I asked you about the meeting in June in Pristina that you said was of the Joint Command, and I asked you whether you had described Sreten Lukic as being the last hole on -- you said something similar to him being the last hole on a flute, you stated that you had not. You challenged me to obtain the transcript of the interview to show you what your exact words were. I've complied with your request, and we have Exhibit 6D170, which is the transcript from your interview, and we also have the videotape of your interview, which I would ask to be shown beginning -- on the transcript it's line -- it should be the last page of that exhibit, lines 7 through 13, and the video which should hopefully be coming up soon should follow that portion of your interview. And, again, I'm not obtaining anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're getting no translation of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe it's on channel 0, Your Honour. There's -- the floor --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think that's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I still don't understand. We're not getting any translation of this for some reason. Nothing's happening to the transcript. This needs to be translated if it's to be of any value.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Unless there's a mechanism for this being read, it will not appear in the transcript and at the moment it's not -- that's not happening. So the interpreters have to do something to get this into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We also have the transcript available at 6D170, the last page, just that there is two words that were indiscernible. The transcript -- at least the stenographer from the OTP that took the transcript, I assume it was an OTP stenographer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can the interpreters actually not translate the part that matters which we've now had played twice so that it appears in the transcript. Nobody's speaking to me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is not the usual procedure, but the booths will try to do as best we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand. I thought it was normal procedure to translate film, the language on film, for us. And I appreciate that this is being translated as we go along as well, but it -- it really needs to be done, otherwise it will not appear in the transcript, unless there is some other mechanism for getting it into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The recording is very poor and the official transcript of the interview is in existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, we will need to proceed on this occasion on the basis that the transcript that was compiled at the time will be the transcript for the purposes of the trial. How that's to be handled in the registry, I have no idea. I'll leave the -- those that know more about these things to sort it out, but the part of the transcript will have to be supplemented by reference to this official translation that you have in your hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can perhaps maybe ask the witness if he could repeat what he heard himself say on the tape. I don't know if that would help any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you do that, please, Mr. Vasiljevic, the part that matters. Could you repeat the words that you heard at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. It was in a different context. It was in 2001, when we had a conversation. In my statement, as was put to me, it was said that I said something along the line as him being the last hole on the flute, the 13th piglet. I don't know how you translate it to English. It is Serbian jargon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've -- but you accept that that's the language you used at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But not in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Have we reached the end of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you could look at the image on the screen, isn't it correct that that's your notebook in front of you on the picture, November the 23rd, 2001, the notebook you claim you didn't have with you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not a nobody, it is merely a pad in which I noted some things down. My notebook looks quite differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I assume that's the end, Mr. Ivetic, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I had said that that's the -- I must not have been turned on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, it's time for us to break, Mr. Vasiljevic, if you could again go with the usher. We'll resume at 11.15. And, in fact, we'll resume with the other matter at 11.15, assuming the witness is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To hear the rest of the Prosecution application, we shall go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours. [The witness takes the stand].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Mr. Vasiljevic. Just one more counsel to cross-examine before we return to the Prosecution's final part, and that is Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General. My name is Slobodan Zecevic, and I am representing Mr. Milan Milutinovic. I have a couple of questions for you, in fact, I will ask for your clarifications and comments on what you said yesterday in your evidence. It is the position of Mr. Milutinovic's Defence that on the basis of the Serbian constitution and all the relevant legal provisions regulating this issue and all the known facts, the President of Serbia, Mr. Milan Milutinovic, had no jurisdiction over the executive branch of the government, including all the ministers in that government and the minister of the interior. In your testimony, yesterday, on page 9122, page [as interpreted] 20 through 25, you said,"According to my logic, the MUP was subordinated to President Milutinovic and then Vlajko Stojiljkovic was in Serbia and Milutinovic was its president." I assume that you were not very precise in what you said.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the Minister of the Interior is part of the cabinet of the Republic of Serbia; but from the point of view of a meeting that is chaired by Milosevic and Mr. Milutinovic was the member of the Supreme Defence Council, this is the context in which I said this. And I thought that it would be quite natural for him to be at that meeting but that Milosevic had not invited him. This is all I have to say on this issue. I never saw Mr. Milutinovic whenever I went to the command post in the Supreme Command Staff. So it is clear to me that he was not the direct superior of Vlajko Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is precisely the gist. Because the transcript, as it stands now, reads that the MUP was actually subordinated to Mr. Milutinovic and that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I was not very accurate in my depiction of the chain of command. I was more referring to this -- to his position as a member of the Supreme Defence Council, thinking that he should have been present there at this meeting chaired by Milosevic, since the -- on the agenda there were items that were -- that concerned Serbia. But Vlajko Stojiljkovic was directly subordinated to the prime minister, but it is the fact that Mr. Milosevic did have direct contacts with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "him," you mean the late Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that we've now clarified this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Hannis, re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I begin, you had asked a question of me, Your Honour on the 22nd on which January at page 8910 of the transcript, where there was a reference in the witness's statement about the crimes mentioned above in Podujevo, Gnjilane, Izbica, and Djakovica. Your Honour, I can tell you in the statement there are references to the crimes in Gnjilane at paragraphs 38 and 65.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which paragraph is making reference to these crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Paragraph 87.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's paragraph 87 that refers to the above crimes, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And Podujevo and Gnjilane are both mentioned in paragraphs 38 and 65. Izbica is mentioned in paragraph 62, and Djakovica in paragraph 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one related matter that came up during Mr. Ivetic's cross. The witness mentioned signing something from Mr. Nice in 2003. Exhibit 387, tab 8 in the Milosevic trial was a declaration signed by this witness concerning or authenticating certain intercepted communications that related to Croatia and I think Bosnia. So that's the only signed document I have from him in 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And does that appear to have been done in the presence of Mr. Nice or can't you tell?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think so because I think Mr. Nice went over those intercepts with him before the declaration was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, General Vasiljevic, I want to go over some matters with you. First of all, I'm going to go out of order and address first some exhibits that Mr. Ackerman discussed with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit 4D138 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, these are the Rules of Service for the VJ for 1996 that Mr. Ackerman showed you. Do you -- do you know if those were the rules that were in effect in 1998 and 1999 for the VJ?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they were. I have no knowledge of any other versions of the Rules of Service being in force later on, so I assume that these were the ones that were in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the upper right corner I note the English translation says: "Military secret for internal use." Is that a correct translation?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, the VJ was also governed by higher laws than these internal regulations, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That included certain provisions in the federal constitution, the Law on Defence, and the Law on the VJ or the Law on the Army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to show the witness Exhibit P1021, please. Actually, Your Honour, this is the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia from 1992. This is a proposed document that we have reached tentative agreement on with the Defence; however, the copy we have is from a textbook. And the Defence has indicated that they would prefer to use the Official Gazette version, which we don't have but we have agreed to use. I just want to make reference to Article 135, and I believe -- I won't have any disagreement from counsel that it says what we say it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but there is one principal disagreement. On the right-hand side, we have a constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; and on the left-hand side, we have the constitution of the Republic of Serbia, which is a completely, completely different -- two completely different documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think so, Mr. Zecevic. If you just look at the one on the right a bit further, it's constitutions of dependencies and special sovereignties and it goes on down to say, eventually, Republic of Serbia by Albert Blaustein.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but, Your Honour, I think that Mr. Hannis was referring to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia constitution from 1992. I'm not sure if my learned colleague wants to use the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That would suggest that he's got the wrong one on both sides of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour for this clarification. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm checking, Your Honour. The ERN doesn't match up with what I believe this was, but perhaps I can have an agreement from my learned colleagues across the hall. The provision that I'm dealing with is one that provides that the VJ is commanded in war and in peace by the president of the republic in conjunction with decisions taken by the Supreme Defence Council. Now, I believe that's an accurate statement of the constitutional provision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And -- well, if you're content that that's accurate and you then want to base a question on it, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, what I've just stated, is that your understanding of what the constitutional provision was about who commanded the army in Yugoslavia in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have already told you what I know. On the basis of the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, President Milosevic had direct command; and the executive persons below him were the Chief of General Staff and in wartime the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to Exhibit P985, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this next one is the Law on Defence from 1994, as published in the Official Gazette of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 5 of the English, I'm looking for Article 40 and 41. And I'm not sure if that's page 5 or 6 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, were you familiar or acquainted with the provisions of the Law on Defence as it related to who commanded the army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not acquainted with this in particular, so that means that I did not have this Official Gazette. I did not study it in depth, but I can give you my interpretation of what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, would you look at Article 40 and item number 2, which -- this is talking about the role of the president of the republic. And it says: "Commands the Army of Yugoslavia in wartime and peacetime." Is that consistent with your understanding at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous answer, this is what I said, and here it says: "In accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council." In other words, the president commands the forces in peace and wartime, the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in Article 41, which talks about the Supreme Defence Council, number 1 is adopt the country's defence plan?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on the English, we'll have to go to the next page, page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it also says it: "Renders decisions in accordance with which the president of the republic commands the Army of Yugoslavia." Is that also consistent with your understanding of who commanded the army in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it does correspond. It is consistent, but here the role of the Supreme Defence Council is outlined in quite specific terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And before we leave that article, if we could go back to page 1, Article 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, General, what was your understanding about who could make a decision about whether or not to declare a state of war, imminent threat of war, or a state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this decision is made by the Assembly at the proposal of the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see Article 4 on the screen -- actually, I guess it's on the bottom of the left column and continuing on to the top. Which says: "If it determines that the sovereignty territory independence constitution or security of the country are under threat, the Federal Assembly shall proclaim one of those states." And I think that's what you just said, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to Exhibit P984, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This, General, is the decree on the proclamation of the law of the army as published in the Official Gazette. This is also from 1994. Were you familiar with the Law on the Army, as regards what it says about who commands the army in war and peacetime?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to object to this line of questioning on several grounds. First of all, it doesn't arise out of cross-examination; but more importantly on the first day of testimony of this witness he said that when he was re-activated, he had not studied -- re-activated in 1999, he had not studied the constitutions or the legislation we're talking about now. He could speak about what he experienced first-hand. You sustained that objection, Your Honour, and here we are back exploring this with this witness and he's -- in fairness to him, he can't answer the questions. He's told Mr. Hannis again this morning he's not comfortable or in a position to speak to these matters. These are matters as he -- as the witness himself has said are for an expert on the law and the constitution. This is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, what's the purpose of this examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Exhibit 4D138 is one that Mr. Ackerman went through with the witness, apparently trying to suggest that General Perisic and later General Ojdanic could use the army basically any way they saw fit if it regarded dealing with terrorist, sabotage, or other armed groups. And I'm using this to say that was language in the army internal regulations, but that was superseded by the Law on Defence, the Law on the Army, and the federal constitution. And this witness, as a 30-year member of the army, should have a pretty good idea of who could command the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was making no such contention. What I was contending was - and it was very clear - that that rule permitted General Perisic to issue that kind of an order without the declaration of a state of emergency, which Mr. Hannis contends is constitutionally required. Now, if he wants to contest something I did, let him show us the portion of the constitution that requires a declaration of emergency before the army can be used in that way. I don't think it exists. That's what I was contending, not that these rules were there. Of course they were there. I never contended they weren't, but I don't change my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I assumed initially that these questions were a prelude to something else. It's not appropriate to explore matters of law with this witness in the way which it's being done at the moment; and therefore, we sustain the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, then could we go to Exhibit 4D138, paragraph 473. I guess we'll have to go to the second page of the B/C/S for the witness to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is an article that talks about the use of army units and institutions in a time of peace. Article 473 purports that: "Army units may be used to combat outlawed, sabotage, terrorist, and other armed enemy groups, or to prevent and eliminate a state of emergency as determined by the president of the federal republic ... or the Supreme Defence Council." Now, General, did you understand that the -- well, let me ask you this question, because I think you answered Mr. Ackerman about this. Who could decide on the use of the army? Who was the authority that could decide on the use of the army? What person or what body was that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One thing that I know for sure on the basis of my experience and what we actually all know as active-duty servicemen, I know that the Chief of General Staff, that his immediate superior is the president of the republic, and I am sure that he cannot use the army without the approval of the president of the republic. And the president of the republic makes decisions of the use of the army on the basis of the Supreme Defence Council. This is actually what I already stated in general, but I did not read or study those articles or paragraphs. This is based on my general knowledge of the service. So the Chief of General Staff is not an independent organ able to make independent decisions on the use and deployment of the armed forces in the field. He cannot decide to take the arms -- army out of the barracks and the decision to use the army to fight certain terrorist groups in the field. This actually leaves open the possibility for the army to be used in case of any internal problems, because the MUP is, in fact, in charge of dealing with any internal problems while the army has to protect the country and protects its sovereignty. But when such groups appear, it is then possible, on the basis of this article, to deploy the army, apart from the MUP. But the decision to use the MUP -- the army or not is not taken by the Chief of General Staff but by the president of the republic, who in turn makes such decisions on the basis of the opinions taken by the Supreme Defence Council. This is my interpretation, and I cannot go any further than this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, we would tender Exhibit P984 and direct the Court's attention to Article 4 which supports what the witness just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, one has to doubt the value of what the witness has said, Mr. Hannis, because the rules are for us to interpret. And, again, we are in territory, I think, that is not helpful to us. But what is P984?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the gazette -- Official Gazette version of the decree of the Law on the Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can we --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Article 4 is the president -- we can put it up on e-court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was 985 we had earlier. 984, I presume, is a different one?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 984 was the Law on the Army; 985 is the Law on Defence. They have similar provisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let us see the provision in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 of the English, it's Article 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Article 4 states: "The president of the republic shall command the army in war and peace in accordance with the decisions of the supreme council," and then: "In his command of the army, the president shall," number 3, "decide on the deployment of the army and approve the plan for its use."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may I may move to exhibit -- I see two counsel on their feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Help me with one thing. Who makes the Rules of Service?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's in Article 4, number 7. The president promulgates those rules that are the Rules of Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, this is open to endless argument that 4D138, the Rules of Service, were in fact made by the president in accordance with a decision of the Supreme Defence Council. And these are matters that will be dealt with as matters of law in due course. They are not matters, I repeat, to be explored further with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, are you saying that P984 has not previously been exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it a document on which you would like --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It has been admitted on the 10th of October, pursuant to the Court's order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I just wanted to say for the sake of the Court and Mr. Hannis, these two laws, the Law on the VJ and the Law on Defence, are -- we are in agreement that the Official Gazette version are in evidence or shall be in evidence very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My notes indicate that they actually are in evidence based on your October 10th decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And what we've done is reviewed with the Prosecution to make sure that the Official Gazette version is, in fact, the one in evidence. And our position, as you have stated several times, this is not the witness to look at these things. And the rules of -- the regulations on the use of the army, if it can assist Mr. Hannis, at the beginning of those rules, it clearly states that those rules are promulgated in accordance with the Law on the VJ and they were brought into force by the president of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we also know, of course, that the witness in his evidence in cross-examination by Mr. Ackerman did explain the circumstances in which he thought this might apply, and he distinguished these circumstances from a state of emergency or from the use of much larger groups. That's something to be evaluated in the light of all other evidence at a later stage. But that was the sort of factual information that was of some use to the Bench. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next could we show the witness 4D137.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General Vasiljevic, this is General Perisic's directive of 28 July 1998, issued about five days after his letter, Exhibit P717, where he complained about the misuse of the army. On this document, I have a couple of questions about some items at the top of the page. On the left, there is a reference to the first administration. Can you explain to the Judges what the first administration is within the VJ.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first administration is the operative administration that elaborates, plans, and documents regarding the use of military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on the right we see a reference to GROM-98, G-R-O-M-98. Do you know what that is?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a code within the war plan, probably. But it can also refer to a special situation outside the war plan that pertains to the use and engagement of the Army of Yugoslavia in terms of protecting the state border, as it is stated here. So that is the code-name of this document, and all documents pertaining to that are coded as GROM-98. So in the roughest possible terms, this is a big file containing all of these documents; this directive, the maps, the plans of the communications and signals units, and everything else that accompanies this kind of directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And state secret-R. Do you know what the R refers to? It says: "Defence state secret-R."

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said. It pertains to war planning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: War is "rat," r-a-t.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in explaining or answering Mr. Ackerman the other day, you indicated, in your view, this was a planning document not an order to carry out an attack as of the date of this order.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could not see when these actions started and when the army was engaged. This is a plan of use, and I've explained that even now there are plans for the use of units under this kind of code, R. Now, when this will actually be applied depends on a specific order. As for this directive, it should be viewed as a plan and it has to be verified by the president of Yugoslavia with his signature that he approves of all of this documentation that accompanies this directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And regarding some of the deployments talked about in this order, there is reference to "as per a special order from the General Staff." But there is no reference to an order number or a date. If indeed this were an operational plan to actually begin attacking or to begin combat, wouldn't there be a reference to a particular order number or a date?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Maybe we need to go to the second page so I can show the general a specific reference of what I just talked about and of the English, too, please. I'm sorry, I think we have to go to page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, under Article 2.1, this is directions for the 3rd Army, and the second paragraph which talks about: "Through quick actions coordinated with the forces of the MUP, overwhelm and destroy, sabotage and terrorist forces as per a special order from the Yugoslav Army's General Staff." Do you see that reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we may have to go back to the next page -- the prior page of the B/C/S. It's Article 1.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: No, it's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that now, I see that part, that it pertains to special order from the Yugoslav Army's General Staff. But, again, this order has to be issued in accordance with approval of the president of the republic.
