I've already said that the army can't be used within the country in combat operations without the approval of the president of the republic, and the president of the republic, again on the basis of the conclusions of the Supreme Defence Council. That is what I've been repeating here time and again. The directive means, as I've already said, that it is a strategic document. It pertains to tasks affecting the Army of Yugoslavia as a whole, and the subordinate commanders elaborate this through concrete forms; that is to say, through their own orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to show you another exhibit now, number 4D122, which Mr. Ackerman showed you yesterday. This is from General Pavkovic as commander of the 3rd Army to the Main Staff on the 29th of April, 1999. Mr. Ackerman showed this to ask you about some references to the criminal cases being referred.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to go to page 2 of the English and of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to the second page of the B/C/S. It's -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's above item number 3. I believe it's four bullet points above -- five bullet points above number 3, and it's a paragraph that begins in English saying: "While searching the terrain and crushing the SDS."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we have to scroll up on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It indicates that: "Measures were taken to block the said sectors and resolve task in the spirit of the decision of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." This is in connection with searching the terrain and crushing Albanian terrorist forces in the Malo Kosovo area. Do you recall, General, the Joint Command order for crushing terrorist forces in the Malo Kosovo area that we looked at on your direct examination, which included an amendment signed by General Lazarevic related to that area?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, this is a report from General Pavkovic to the General Staff of the army or the Supreme Command Staff, including the reference to the Joint Command. Now, I want to ask you about Exhibit 4D125. This is a 1st of August, 1998, document from the 3rd Army. General Samardzic was in command at the time. And this is an order to the commander of the Pristina Corps personally, General Pavkovic, with regard to a request of the Joint Command for engagement of Pristina Corps units. And General Samardzic forbids the use of those Pristina Corps units, pending the approval of the plan for the execution of the third phase in the office of the FRY president on 3 August and his preliminary approval on the 2nd of August. Can you explain that to us. This is dated the 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what this would pertain to. At any rate, he is saying that the third phase should not start before verification is obtained from the president of Yugoslavia. That is how I understand it. I don't know what his previous information of the 2nd of August refers to. I cannot interpret it. I don't know what it was that was going on before that, what decisions they made, and whether he is now withdrawing that decision until it is verified by the president, and that is moving on to the third stage. Now, one can also go back and analyse what the third stage is. I think that the third stage is a more massive engagement on the part of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to next go to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: These are two documents, Your Honour, that Mr. Ackerman did not show the witness, but they were included on the list that we received for cross-examination, 4D100 and 4D119, that I would like to show the witness. First of all, 4D100.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, while we're waiting for that, yesterday at page 53, line 9, you mention a unit that had rebelled and left Kosovo to go to Krusevac. This was in May 1999, before your trip to Kosovo. Do you recall what unit that was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 7th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the military territorial unit from Brus as well and Aleksandrovac, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that relates and corroborated testimony of K73.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This document, this is K -- this is 4D100 from the 22nd of July, 1998. This is from General Pavkovic to his superior, General Samardzic, regarding engagement of the Pristina Corps. Could you read that, General. It's -- he makes reference to: "At the meeting with the President of the FRY in his office on the 21st of July, an order was given to implement the plan for combatting terrorist ... "The plan envisages the participation of MUP and Pristina Corps units ... "In view of the above, please work out in more detail the engagement of the Pristina Corps units in implementation of the plan." This is from the subordinate officer to the superior, and it appears to be directing his superior to work out details of the plan. Is that common in an order from a subordinate to a superior?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't understand it as an order. I understand it as a request that he be given more specific tasks, because probably in this plan for combatting the terrorist forces those tasks had not been spelled out with sufficient precision in the view of General Pavkovic. So he had the right to seek more complete information and more precise orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Typically would that be worded as a request, request for clarification or a request for further orders?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that this form is not contrary to practice or to regulations. He is addressing him and seeking more precise tasks. It would be of interest to see what the response of the army command was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look at Exhibit 4D119.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you're following my train of thought. This is also on the same day, the 22nd of July, 1998, from General Samardzic to General Pavkovic. And it appears to be the response, and he reflects. It says: "The president approved on the 21st of July the plan for the second phase as you General Pavkovic had personally proposed it. "In view of the above, now General Samardzic is requesting a proposal regarding the engagement of the Pristina Corps." Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may give a free interpretation here, I have the impression that the commander of the Pristina Corps and the army commander are corresponding with each other, and probably both understand what is to be done. He is saying here that it was precisely General Pavkovic who presented the plan of use at that meeting, and he believes therefore that there is no need for him to elaborate it for him. Now he is asking for a concrete proposal so that he could verify it for him, so that he'd have sufficient elements for making a decision. That's how I interpret it. I cannot be a direct witness, but what I remember is that there was a problem there, up there in the top echelons of the General Staff. Because at the meeting with President Milosevic, they accepted these decisions. And as far as I heard, later on they would say to General Pavkovic that he should not carry that out because the state of emergency had not been declared, so don't go for engagement, and then he asked for decided orders. People who told me about this say that he said: "Well, why did you keep silent while we were at the meeting there, and now you are forbidding me to engage forces without your specific approval." Now, whether this discussion has to do with the situation that we see here now, I don't know. But that is what I had been told, and I told you that there were these two people who told me about this. Whether that's correct, I don't know, and I don't know to what extent it is correct, if so. However, there were analyses as to how the army should be used and for what. I believe at these meetings General Pavkovic was present; I assume that he was present. And he was directly given a task then to go into action in terms of the second stage of the plan, and he's the one who had proposed that stage before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did your sources who told you about this indicate whether or not General Samardzic had been at the meeting with the president?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Samardzic, Perisic, and I think General Dimitrijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what about General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I want to show you Exhibit P1439.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Ackerman and Your Honours should know this was not on our list of exhibits we intended to show, but it is one I think has been raised because of the questions on cross-examination. Mr. Ackerman offered the general's personnel rating and talked about how he abided by the chain of command. I think it has some bearing on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is from the 5th of October, 1998, from General Pavkovic to General Samardzic regarding the Joint Command and the formation of rapid intervention units. General, can you see item number 1? It says: "Contrary to your orders, Pristina Corps command has not formed any new combat groups." Under what circumstances was it permissible for a subordinate to disobey an order of a superior commander?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, orders have to be carried out. Only if they are contrary to the constitution and laws and constitute a serious violation, then it is the duty of the subordinate to warn the superior of that; and then he will not carry out only that order which would constitute a grave criminal offence. As for all others, they have to be carried out. Now, what is this here? I don't think that there is any controversy here. It was just stated that the Pristina Corps had not formed these new combat groups yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you look at -- and the paragraph right above item number 3, the English is translated as saying: "As part of the conclusions from the ZK," which in the context and as has been translated elsewhere is the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija meeting, "I sent you the decision to form rapid intervention forces which you forebade in your order on the such-and-such of October." Can you give us any comment on what, if anything, this says about the relative relations between the 3rd Army, the Pristina Corps, and the Joint Command? Who's in charge or can you tell?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the commander of the 3rd Army still has jurisdiction over the command of the Pristina Corps. And if you read this, the first paragraph, it says here that the Pristina Corps did not form combat groups in contravention of your order, and the order actually forebade the establishment, the formation, of such groups. And they were not formed and this was not in contravention; in other words, the order was complied with. And now when it goes on to say the conclusions from the ZK, "I sent you the decision to form rapid intervention forces," this means that he sent the decision, yet he was forbidden from actually doing that. I think that this is still the stage at which they have this correspondence and the actually operations have not yet started, the army commander forbid this. And at the meeting with Milosevic, he made this decision and he instructed the Pristina Corps commander that the decision was accepted and that he should comply with it; then there was a conflict with General Perisic who wanted a state of emergency to be declared, but it all ended there. He had a dissenting opinion, but he did not tell President Milosevic in no uncertain terms that he forbids the use of this in -- until a decision is made. And General Pavkovic was then in a situation where he had to comply with the orders he received from the president of the republic, as the commander under the constitution. When he went back to Pristina, he received a memo, a letter, to the effect that this should not be done; and then he said, "Why did you keep quiet at the meeting?" And I think this is evidence of this dualism. This is what I learned at the meeting, and this is in line with what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now I want to move on to some of Mr. Visnjic's cross-examination. One of the documents he showed you was Exhibit 3D481.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't need that on the screen I don't think for this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This regarded the induction of volunteers and the standard for them. You mentioned that psychological testing and screening was part of the process in 1999. Do you know the nature of testing that was done for would-be volunteers. Was that filling out a questionnaire? Was that an interview with the psychologist? Was that a ten-minute affair or was that a two-day affair? Do you know how that was done?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it was done. I know how it is usually done. You give a person a test; and then, if necessary, a more detailed examination is carried out. I don't know what methodology was applied here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do want to show you next Exhibit 3D482. This is the 16th April 1999 document entitled, "Warning" from General Ojdanic. Do you recall that one?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you already made some comment about it, but my question was: Is a warning a standard kind of military order?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, this warning is an order. Its purpose is preventive, lest somebody should do something that would contravene any previous orders. So this is, in fact, placing an emphasis on how things should be done, but this is not a standard document of -- that has a standard format that is contained in the list of documents produced by the staff. But it depends on what the warning is all about. So it is a reminder on the following -- the previous documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about Exhibit P1487, if we could look at that. This is from, I believe, the 17th of April, 1999, from the General Staff, and this one is translated in the English as "suggestions to the 3rd Army." And I guess I have a similar question. Are suggestions a typical kind of military document from a commander to subordinates?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this order was not mentioned in the examination-in-chief, and it is already contained in the statement of this witness. And I don't see the point that Mr. Hannis wishes to make here; in other words, I think I did not mention this in my cross-examination. I did not do that and it is already in the statement, so I don't know what Mr. Hannis wants to achieve through this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the point arising from cross, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this relates -- he was asked about the warning document, and I'm trying to make a -- I'm trying to join these two things, warning and suggestions, and how they are to be interpreted by subordinates in terms of whether or not that's an order that needs to be complied with or whether it can be ignored in the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right, you can proceed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's my question, General. I don't know if you answered. Are suggestions from a superior to subordinate a typical kind of military document that you would see?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that basically orders would be typical documents, but I can see this link between the order of the Joint Command dated the 15th. This -- the reference is to this order and the actual date of this document is the 17th. And I have this impression that there was a -- there was some extraordinary circumstances that prompted them to react in this way. I cannot explain what happened, but a suggestion was made because the order of the Joint Command dated the 15th already was in existence, so two days earlier than this document. Now, whether this order had already been executed or had yet to be executed, I don't know. But some remarks were made of a practical nature relating to this order, and some practical suggestions were made as to how to supplement and implement this order. It has a certain legal weight; and if any damage was to be -- to result from the previous order of the Joint Command and if the 3rd Army had not accepted the suggestions, then the commander would suffer the consequences of the failure to do so. So this is a suggestion made in good will how to do this because this is from the superior command. There could have been a direct order; but because of the existence of an order of a superior command, this was done in a more flexible manner. So it was a suggestion made to the 3rd Army. Had I been the commander of the 3rd Army, I would have accepted the suggestions and I would have corrected the orders that I had issued accordingly. Because it implies a certain obligation to comply with these suggestions, but it is not as strong as it is in the case of an order. In the previous case, there was an explicit order "I forbid the use," and so on, by General Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he was shown it on direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you saw it in -- before you saw it the other day, had you seen this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I had not. I don't know what year it is. Yeah -- no, I hadn't seen it regardless the fact that it is dated 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you ever before seen a document between two commands headed "suggestions"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the answer you've just given your speculation about this document, or is there any foundation for the answer you've just given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that this is not the usual format for the communication with one's subordinates. Subordinates are issued orders, loud and clear. And this is a little bit more peculiar because a suggestion is given, but it does imply a certain obligation. The -- to my mind, the subordinate is under the obligation to comply with it. It is just a nuance in terms of how it is actually styled.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, just a clarification, not regarding this. Mr. Hannis said that this document was shown to the witness in the examination-in-chief, and I'm sure that we all missed it if that was the case. When was it shown? This is what I wanted to ask. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to check the transcript. It was on my handwritten list and checked off, but I can't tell you now I remember specifically when I showed it. I have to search the transcript, if I can do that during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, the witness should not be examined on this document until you have been able to prove that you have actually shown it to him because none of us here remember that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw this document. This document was shown to me, but I don't know when it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I don't think that is a rule that applies. The only question is whether the document's relevant to the issue that counsel is exploring at the moment, and that that is something which arose from cross-examination and we've already determined that to be the case. The clarification you seek, though, would be helpful for me as well, and we'll get it after the break. Now, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, one last question then. Can you tell us anything about the fact that the Supreme Command is giving suggestions to its subordinate, the 3rd Army command, regarding an order from the Joint Command. Does that tell you anything about how the Supreme Command views orders from the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to have to object. That calls for speculation. Surely, there's no foundation for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that not a matter for argument, Mr. Hannis, in due course?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think it is, Your Honour. But, as a 30-year veteran and army commander who is familiar with subordinate/superior relationships, he may be able to tell us something that we non-professional soldiers would not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think you've established a foundation for this, especially since the document pre-dates his period of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The next Exhibit is 3D479. This was a report to the Supreme Command Staff that Mr. Visnjic showed you. And at page 5 of the English, there is a reference where General Ojdanic is speaking about the task of the UB, your administration. And it says: "Its task is to continue monitoring paramilitary organisations." General, were -- was the UB monitoring paramilitary organisations up to that date, during your time of re-activation? This would seem to suggest this was an ongoing process.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, care was always taken to ensure that paramilitary organisations are not present in the field and to eliminate them or remove them, so this was a permanent obligation; not only on the part of the security organs to do that, to ensure that this is done through their operational work, but also the commanders in the field were supposed to take measures and report up the chain of command. This is a permanent task that was in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And at the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One more question before the break, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the end of this document, there's a reference to Mr. Andjelkovic being at this meeting of the Supreme Command. Would it be unusual for a civilian to be attending a meeting of the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was not Zoran Andjelkovic, but it was General Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the assistant in the communications and electronics sector. So this was not a civilian, it was a general member of the collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That clears up my misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we take the break now. I have about 15 more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've reached lunchtime, Mr. Vasiljevic. I still think we're on track for you finishing today, although a bit later than I thought yesterday. Meanwhile, could you go again with the usher, and we'll see you in an hour at quarter to 2.00. So we adjourn until 1.45. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as the witness is coming in, I can advise you that regarding Exhibit P1487, I have checked the transcript. It was not shown to him by me during his direct testimony. It was discussed at pages 8800 to 8811, when we were discussing all the exhibits that were on my list that I wanted to have admitted and that Mr. Petrovic had objected to. There was no objection to that at that time; and at page 8808, line 11, it was admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The had witness said earlier that he had seen it before. It was an exhibit in the Milosevic trial, at tab 387 -- Exhibit 387, tab 40 and at page 15972, line 18 in the Milosevic transcript. In open session, it was discussed with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Well, you may now continue your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I now want to go into some questions that Mr. Bakrac, counsel for General Lazarevic, asked you. Yesterday, at page 8962, line 22, he was asking you about certain units in Kosovo, and one of them was the 202nd logistics base. You said that was not subordinated to the Pristina Corps. Can you tell us to whom they were subordinated, if you know.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please. The interpreters didn't catch the first part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but I didn't know whether this was directly subordinate to the army, because there was some logistics base that was subordinated to the General Staff. But I do believe that this was the logistics base that belonged to the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know where they were physically located?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac also showed you a couple of daily combat reports from General Lazarevic and the Pristina Corps. One of them was Exhibit 5D85. I don't need to put it on the screen to ask you a question. You confirmed, I think, that it contained all the appropriate and typical entries that there would be in a combat report. One of those is an entry regarding ammunition used during the preceding reporting period. And I think in that case it was item number 7.3, and it indicated that 150 bullets of 7.62 ammunition were used. Would that be the total amount of those bullets used by all the subordinate units of the Pristina Corps for the preceding 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I did not pay much attention to that. Was -- I read the document, but this is probably what is referred to as one combat set that contains 150 rounds. But I would have to look at the document in order to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we bring up 5D85, and if we could go to the page where item 7.3 is. I think we have to go to the third or fourth page of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There you have the B/C/S at the very bottom, General, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that is. Is that 150 bullets or 150 some other kind of units?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 150 bullets for an automatic rifle were used. This is a combat report, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report stating that that is the amount of ammunition used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, these were daily reports, so this would cover a period of 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit 5D84 and go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is another daily combat report, General; and on the signature page, we see the seal and signature. Right above that there are two sets of initials TJ/MT. Do you know what those would be, or who they would be?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who, but it is the person who wrote the report. And the other two initials are the initials of the person who typed out the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now I want to ask you about some of the questions that Mr. Ivetic on behalf of General Lukic asked you. And it -- in spite of the fact that you initially stated in your suspect interview that General Djordjevic was a speaker at the meeting, are you convinced as you sit here in court today that General Lukic, who is here in the courtroom, was the one you saw give the first briefing at that Joint Command meeting in June 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure and I have that noted down in my notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with regard to that, Judge Bonomy asked you if you still had that notebook. Would you be willing to furnish us a copy of your notes from that meeting of the Joint Command in June 1999, only that portion?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, but the procedure has to be observed. I have to be given approval for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, General. Thank you. Now, you mentioned that the Minister of the Interior for the -- for the time-period we've been talking about was Mr. Stojiljkovic. Do you know what his occupation or profession was before he got put in that job?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, one other question I want to clear up. At page 9005, line 6, from yesterday, you were asked by Mr. Ivetic - let me get the exact wording - you were talking about Boca and the Skorpions, and the question was: "And you indicated that they returned to Kosovo. And I take it from the fact that in your testimony, your statement, your interview with the OTP, that insofar as no other incidents were cited pertaining to this group, you have no explicit information that they committed any crime if and when they were redeployed in Kosovo following Podujevo, otherwise you would have mentioned it. Am I correct?" And you said: "Yes." In paragraph 38 of your statement that is in evidence, you make reference to this group or some of this group having returned and committed crimes in Gnjilane. Can you explain that to me, as there seems to be a discrepancy between that answer to Mr. Ivetic and what's in your statement. Can you tell us which is correct.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not said in detail what was done in Gnjilane; however, later on when information was checked the case of the village of Zegra near Gnjilane appeared, and I think it was cleared up who it was who had done that. The first knowledge stated it was the group around Gnjilane; however, when we checked later on it was confirmed that it was in the village of Zegra near Gnjilane, and I do not have any confirmation that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was your information about who the perpetrators were?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zegra you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A paramilitary group. Sorry for having interrupted you. It was a paramilitary group that belonged to the army basically, a group of volunteers I think it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Hannis, we should delete the words "and in Gnjilane"?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, when you say Zegra, that was the only incident you were aware of in the municipality of Gnjilane, but not in Gnjilane itself?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the last thing I want to talk about, Your Honour, I think I need to go into private session for this. This relates to paragraph 87.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. This evidence -- or the evidence in relation to this so far has been in private session and we shall resume private session briefly while we hear this part of the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I previously indicated that I wanted to offer a portion of Exhibit 1898, which is Obrad Stevanovic's diary. And I indicated I wanted to offer a page range that was both before and after the specific items that the witness talks about in paragraph 72 of his statement. Between the 7th of May and the 20th of May are the dates in the diary that I wanted to include. The last -- along the last three or four lines before the 20th of May, there is a reference in General Stevanovic's diary about Fehmi Agani that relates to this. And I wanted to let the Defence know that so that no one thinks I'm trying to sneak that in past them. But there is a reference about that which I think pertains to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could we perhaps get the page number so we can find it quicker. It's a rather bulky document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Let me get that for you. It's pages 106 and 107 of the English, and I believe in the original that's page 89. With that, Your Honour, I have no more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Vasiljevic, Mr. Hannis asked you about the availability of your notebook, and you said that you would require formal approval. What is the status of that notebook? Is it your own private document, or does it belong to someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It is my notebook, but it contains quite a few elements from operative activities; and therefore, it is an official notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think Mr. Hannis's concern only relates to the particular issue that we explored in certain detail, and that was the meeting and the role, if any, played by Mr. Lukic in that meeting. So far as that part of your notebook is concerned, is there any reason why that shouldn't be copied and simply left here before you leave The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that notebook here with me now. I've already said. I did not bring any documents here. The notebook is in Belgrade. And I can submit it to the office there, or I can do it some other way from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking, Mr. Hannis, that it's only that part that you're interested in?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it should be possible to deal with it fairly speedily, Mr. Vasiljevic, and it would be of great assistance to the Tribunal if you were to deal with it immediately on your return to Belgrade. We would be extremely grateful for that. Mr. Hannis, what do you envisage as the time-scale for the submission you were asked to make about other documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could do it by Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, it should be possible for the Defence to respond to that by Tuesday so that we can deal with the matter in the course of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That now completes your evidence, Mr. Vasiljevic. Thank you very much for coming again to the Tribunal to give it, and you're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Since special arrangements have to be put in place for the next witness, we will require to adjourn. We'll adjourn for half an hour and resume at 20 minutes to 3.00. And I understand that parties here in court and the interpreters are willing to continue until 4.00, so that we can make up the time we would otherwise lose. And I'm extremely grateful on behalf of the Bench for that. So we'll resume at 20 minutes to 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To hear the evidence of the next witness, we shall go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me correct what I said a short time ago. We are in open session now. We were in closed session for the witness to enter the courtroom. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. May we indeed go into private session for two initial questions I would like to put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, how many years did you attend school?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you attended elementary school. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did attend secondary school, too, but I never graduated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At which -- around which age did you leave school?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was about 16 and a half, maybe even -- in fact, 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you at some point called up for national military service?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I actually volunteered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the Defence on their feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me to say, we have technical problems. We can't hear on our headphones -- actually, probably, it is a problem with the channels, but we can't hear the witness on our channel. I apologise if I disturbed with this interruption. Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that clear now? And you should be able to follow what's happened so far fairly easily on the transcript with your own knowledge of English. Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, you -- we were talking about military service.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that a service that every young man in your country had to take?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was any part of these 12 months a training period?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, five months and 20 days of infantry training.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long was your training in these 12 months?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you given any reasons why your training was only two months and not, as you said, the regular five months and 20 days?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they didn't tell us why the training had been cut down. Probably at that time because we had to go to Kosovo, because we ordinary soldiers. We didn't know what was happening, and we didn't know why it was shorter than usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during these two months, what was -- what were you trained in? What were the topics the young soldiers would receive training in?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first we learned how to clean our weapons, then target practice, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you receive during this time any training on how to behave towards civilian population, how to treat prisoners of war, or about the laws of war in an armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We did not learn anything about the war, the civilians. This was not an issue, and we were not taught anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you said your training ended because you were sent to Kosovo. When were you first sent to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime in late May, that's when we were sent to Kosovo, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had you ever been to Kosovo before?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge about Kosovo, about the cities there or villages, the geography in general?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard about the towns of Pec and Pristina, but I didn't really know about that. And I had never gone there so I didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in Kosovo, where were you first sent to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we went straight from Valjevo by train to Pristina, and then we were bussed to Djakovica. This was the place that was designated as my location.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were any uniforms issued to you when you arrived in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had kit with us, what we wore on our bodies, and then we were also issued a spare uniform in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you describe how these uniforms looked like, the colour?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The green camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how about weapons, were you also issued weapons when you arrived in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the barracks in Djakovica, where we were issued a rifle, helmet; that's what we were issued with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And upon your arrival in Kosovo, were you given any briefings about what to expect in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you at that point given any instructions or orders or booklets regarding the behaviour in the field, the treatment of the civilian population and prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to go into some details of his unit, and I would like to do that in private session if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the location you were deployed, were there other units than your own; and if so, which ones?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Right at the beginning, I didn't know about any other units because the mortar company was there; and then three or four days later, there was an infantry company there and the 82-millimetre mortar company, the tank unit, and some other units, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how many mortars would a platoon have?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had two. One platoon had two mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how many men would be needed to operate one mortar?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crew would have five or six people; the sixth person would be the driver. So that would be five to six people per each mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And before you were deployed in your position, did you ever receive any training on mortars before?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had never seen a mortar in Valjevo at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So who told you how to operate them in the field? How did you know what to do?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a previous generation of soldiers there who had gone to the front line, and the mortars were already in position. So we simply worked alongside them. There was no time for us to undergo any training. We simply learnt from them. We would observe them, and then they would tell us. When they did not have to open fire, they would tell us, This is how you do it, this is how you do it, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the time you arrived at this location in May or early June 1998, were these mortars fired? Were they used?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That night when we got there, no fire was opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think my question was not clear. From that time onwards, let's say from June 1998 onwards, were the mortars used?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how often would you and the others be asked to fire these mortars?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depended. Sometimes it would be at night and in the day, and then a night would go by without any fire. It would all depend on what the infantry would ask for fire support.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the range of the mortars you operated?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had 9 to 70 kilometres [as interpreted], and everything would depend on the charge, on the actual charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you again because I'm not sure. Could you again say what was the range.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the range would depend on the charge, the actual shell used. 980, 70 [as interpreted] kilometres. When -- I don't know. I would sometimes ask the actual charge that was used and the actual shell that was used, but I think the longest range was 980 or 970 [as interpreted] kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The record's becoming horribly confused. There's not a mortar that I know of that will shoot 70 or 80 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a matter for exploration in evidence. It's all to do with the reliability of the witness. Just let the--

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not what he's saying. He's 9.7 and 9.8 and 9.9. He's not saying 980 or 970.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You mean that's what he's saying in B/C/S, and it's being wrongly translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. He's putting a decimal point between the 9 and the 7 or a comma as might be the case in some places. He's not saying that there's a mortar that fires 70 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understood that, too. But just exactly what it was is not clear. But if you're saying if it's 9.7 and 9.8 that's not being properly translated, then I need to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would actually would have been my next question, because as you see I asked him twice because I noted that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, to clarify that, do you mean 9.7 or 9.8 kilometres, so less than 10 kilometres was the range, the firing range?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With this range in mind, did you actually see what you were firing at when you were operating the mortars, or was it out of your sight?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was impossible because that was over the hill. We were unable to see our target and to see what is it that we're actually firing on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you learn at some point, nevertheless, where you were directing mortar fire at?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew on one occasion that the target was actually the mosque and that the KLA troops were there, that they had their stronghold there, and that they were returning fire on our infantry; and that's why we were asked to fire on this target, but that was just once and that was the only occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you learn where this mosque was, in which village?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the village of Smolnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for how long did you stay in this position and to fire mortars at this village, Smolnica?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, three or four, four and a half months, that's how long we were there with fire sometimes more frequently. Sometimes there would be a lull of maybe one or two days, but everything depended on the actual developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there a period when there was particularly heavy mortar fire, when you were using it particularly often?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in August or September, I don't know what the exact date was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that would still be in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during the month you were operating the mortar in the direction of Smolnica, were there other artillery units also shooting in this direction?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were in some positions around us, but I don't know exactly what we were targeting and I couldn't look at what other people were doing. We had to focus on our targeting and firing. However, I heard stories from others. When they would return, they would encounter the odd soldier here and there and then they would tell us things. One of such soldiers was a member of the tank unit, but I never saw something myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did this soldier of the tank unit tell you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked about it. I asked him if they were under a lot of pressure, and I said we were targeting something yesterday. And he said, We were targeting something as well, but I don't know whether we were shooting at the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After the three or four or four and a half months that you said you stayed at this location, where were you deployed next?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were sent to another position at Zub.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what were your tasks there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same. We used the mortars at our positions, and the direction of our firing was more or less the same towards Smolnica, I think. The tasks were not changed once we were deployed to Zub.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How did you know that you were firing in the same direction?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, soldiers were talking about it. We knew we were targeting Smolnica again because it was a stronghold of the KLA. They were dug-in there, and we were told that our infantry cannot pass because of that. And usually after five or six days I would learn about the exact location, and this was the case on this occasion as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see other units in Zub, artillery or infantry or any other?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was infantry. We were always close to them. I don't know whether a tank unit was there. There may have been, but we and the infantry moved along together. Maybe they were with us as well, but I truly don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Zub with these tasks?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were there until the 24th of March when NATO began its air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at this point did you and other soldiers with you receive any specific orders?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Our 120 mortar unit was ordered to provide two mortars of

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: to remain in Kosovo and that their identification papers were to be torn, so as to prevent them from coming back.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would request two redactions in the past minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, I see the registrar nodding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I don't want to draw attention to them, but maybe if we could communicate them in written form.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: May I continue in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment until we deal with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, we left off talking about the orders you received. What did you understand these orders to mean? And I would ask you not to mention names any more, if you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you understand the question? What did you understand the order to mean?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I presume it meant that no Albanians were to remain. It was my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after these instructions were given, where were you then sent?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to Orahovac and its surroundings, the villages there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said previously that you -- that you went to Djakovica. Was that a mistake or ...

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were at the positions at Zub towards Djakovica, and then we went towards Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what were your tasks in the Orahovac area when you were deployed there? What did you have to do there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To search houses and to seize ammunition if any was found as well as weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How would such searches be conducted? Which units would participate in such searches?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The infantry were always in front of us. We covered their back. In case they would run into trouble, we would provide mortar support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to just go back slightly on this. You said that your commander ordered you to go with 20 men to a particular place and said something about not a single Albanian ear to be left in Kosovo. Now, which place was it you were told to go at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Towards Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies it. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned the infantry went first. Who do you include in the infantry? Who was part of this infantry?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The infantry -- well, I don't know who exactly. Those who were issued with automatic rifles and machine-guns. They did not have heavy pieces. That's the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was this only VJ soldiers in this group you call infantry or were there also police --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, this is really leading and according to us wouldn't have any probative value after this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I agree with that. I think that should have been an open question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: May I reformulate that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were there any other units than the VJ involved in these searches or any other groups?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was the police and some wearing blue camouflage uniforms and Balaclavas. A friend told me that they were Arkan's Tigers. Other than that, I had no idea who they were. They had blue berets, green berets, the police, the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How did the -- which uniforms did the police wear?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where were they in relation to the searches --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In relation to the searches conducted, where would you see police officers?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went with the infantry, but not together but to the other side; however, they went in together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned the other persons in blue uniform -- blue camouflage uniforms, Balaclavas and blue berets, and that you were told by a friend that they were Arkan's Tigers. Was it the first time you saw these particular people during the searches after the NATO bombing started in 1999, or had you seen them before somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had seen them sometime in 1998 when we were on the road to Smolnica. Up until that moment, I had never seen them. I never had any contact. I didn't know who they were until that friend told me who they actually were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in relation to all these other people you just described, where was your unit and where were you when the searches were conducted?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We always followed them. We were a hundred metres behind. We always followed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During the searches, did you also see people participating who would not wear any kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were such people. I don't know whether they were civilians or soldiers or reservists, but there were such people, no uniform, but sporting a weapon and they would usually -- or they would usually wear a VJ uniform as well [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, the last answer is not quite clear. You said: "No uniform, but sporting a weapon and they would usually ... wear a VJ uniform." Can you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. They did not have any uniforms; we did, the VJ. They wore civilian clothes and had weapons. They did not have VJ uniforms as we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would they be together with any of the other groups that you described, or were they separate from them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were with the infantry and police group.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you regarding discipline in the units as you observed it yourself. Was there a difference between the discipline among soldiers and other people you observed partaking in these searches in 1998 and in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The discipline was very good until NATO began with air-strikes. Soldiers were supposed to be dressed properly in those conditions, but later it changed. Some people were getting drunk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during these searches, did you observe any -- any people who appeared to be drunk?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in our group. Our commander was tough and our group was okay, but some others behaved improperly. There were drunken people around.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know members of which group they were? Were they from the -- were they soldiers? Police? Or Arkan's Tigers? Or these civilians that you described, if you can say?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Maybe they were soldiers or reservists, those who had served their military term. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you observe this behaviour about people who wore a uniform, what uniform whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. Among the regular soldiers such cases were infrequent; they behaved in a better way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many villages did you approximately search in this way, together with the other units?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I did not keep count. There were many villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you think about it and try to be a bit more specific. Are we talking about two or three or ten or more?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, a couple of things. That last is a bit leading, but my major concern is we have no time-frame at all. I don't know if she's asking about searches in 1998, 1999. I have no idea when these are. It's very difficult to deal with them if you don't have some time-frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My assumption is this is after the bombing has started, but perhaps you can clarify the period we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the witness has never said after the bombing started. That was something the Prosecutor threw in, after the bombing started, but the witness has never said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness said he was sent to Orahovac only after the NATO bombing started and that this was then his task. I thought the time-frame was clear, but I can ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have him noted as saying that they were in the Zub until the 24th of March when the air-strikes began, and I think these are his own word.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree with that, Judge, until we went a little further along and then Ms. Moeller says that -- she's asking him questions about 1998 and 1999 again. And so then I don't know if we're -- which spot we're in. I can find the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: She will clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The only reference I've noted thereafter to 1998 was that that's when the witness had first seen these irregularly clad people when he was on the road to Smolnica, but we can clarify it. Ms. Moeller, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, we were talking about the different discipline in 1998 and 1999, and can you tell me about the discipline in 1999 during the searches. What is your testimony in regards to that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said it was so before the NATO air-strikes. Everything was fine in 1998. Up until the 4th of March, the discipline was okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the 24th, however, things changed once the air-strikes began, and then all sorts of things began taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The intervention, though, from Mr. Ackerman came when you were being asked how many villages you had searched in this particular way. Now, when you're talking about searching villages, what period of time are we talking about? Are we talking about before or after the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can you be even more specific about the period in which you were involved doing this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] NATO began bombing on the 24th, and then on that day, around midnight or 1.00 or 2.00 in the morning, we were told to pack up. And early in the morning, around 5.00, 5.30, on the 25th we set off towards Djakovica and Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how many villages did you search in this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly. I cannot recall. Not one or two, more. I could venture a guess. I don't dare say seven or five, however more than three. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Over what period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the 24th of March, we stayed there for some 20 or 22 or 23 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In that period that we were just talking about or we are talking about, were you ever asked or ordered to assist the police with anything?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While you were in the Orahovac area, did you ever receive an order from your commander that you should assist the police with anything?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were asked to do something concerning the mortars. They had two 82-millimetre mortars. We were asked to instruct them how to work with the shells, level, and the coordinates. All they knew to do was to turn the barrel to the right or to the left, depending on where they were supposed to fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did the police have, to your knowledge, a specific mortar platoon or a mortar unit as the army would?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know of it. Had they had it, they would probably have known how to work with mortars, just as we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So how did they use the mortars in the searches?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't remember that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- that anybody mentioned that mortars were used in searches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we've had evidence that the mortars were used in some form of back-up during the search. How that was done is not clear, but that evidence we've had so far, I think. Because this witness wasn't involved in the searches as I understand it. So you can deal with it in cross-examination. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, the question was if there wasn't any specific unit in the police for the mortars, how did they use it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly whether they had a mortar company. They used mortars firing at a certain -- in a certain direction on that day, and they asked our commander to assist them, to help them with operating them. They fired perhaps three or four rounds because there was some automatic fire coming from that direction targeting them, and they asked for some assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think the question is in relation to you with the mortar unit. Were the mortars close to where you would be in the arrangement of the units, or would they be somewhere else at some other location?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mortars were behind us. The mortars were usually on the trucks; and in case our infantry needed assistance, we would take them off and use them. The mortars were always with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So this is your mortars you're talking about, the mortars of the army or also the mortars of the police?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Army; it's the army that has mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the police mortars you were speaking about, were they also on some trucks, or where were they in relation to where you and your mortars were?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were ahead of us, this mortar 82. There would be three or four men who would be in charge of that, then they'd have to carry the tripod, then have to carry the barrel, because the 82s were not hooked on to trucks. They had to be carried.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said that you cannot say the exact number of villages you participated in searching. Do you recall any village name of these villages that you passed through with the rest of the army and the other forces?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember. Quite a few Albanian villages. I don't know. I could just say this or that, but I really cannot remember. It's been quite a while. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. During these searches, did you ever see any killings being committed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there would be columns of refugees and then they would separate the men from women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall when -- approximately when you observed that, that men were separated from women and children from a convoy?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was in April. Was it mid-April? It was then; it was in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what happened to these men after they were separated?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the men were lined up. They had some KLA uniform and they ordered them to put it on, and then they killed them in order to prove that they were not killing innocent people, civilians, but that they were members of the KLA army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who had some KLA uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they did. They -- it was the Army of Yugoslavia. Now, how come they had them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say "the Army of Yugoslavia." Can you be more specific. Do you know who were the men who had the uniforms, and who did what you just testified to? What uniforms would they wear?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms did these men wear?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These who were separating the men. I mean these people were just civilians, regular people, and it was our army, our infantry, that was separating them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How did you know it was men from the infantry, from the VJ infantry, who was doing that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew one of them. One of these men was with me in Valjevo and he was trained with me personally, and I knew him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this person who was in the training with you, what did he do exactly or what did you see him do?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw exactly. We in the army call this the machine-gun, and then there was this box for it that we called Ceca; we, the soldiers, did. And he fired that machine-gun and killed these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And these people, who were they, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were Albanians, civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of clothes did they wear, initially?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you see yourself that they were given these KLA uniforms, as you say, and ordered to put on before they were shot?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that. There was that little hill there, and we would always guard their backs. I didn't hear the order, Put on those clothes. If they had their civilian clothes off and these uniforms on, there must have been an order to make that happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how many men that you say appeared to be Albanian civilians were killed this way?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I wasn't counting, but there was this line, as they were lined up, it was a long line. Now, how many of them there were exactly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you give a rough estimate. Was it a small group or a large group?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe 20-ish, maybe a bit more. Something like that. There was this line and maybe there were even more of them. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And the VJ soldier that you knew from before, do you know his name or nickname?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just know his nickname, Zemunac. I don't know his real name. He probably came from Zemun or maybe he just had this nickname pertaining to Zemun. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After the men were killed, were shot, could you observe what happened then?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was this event the only one of its nature that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. One more time. But who was killing them and doing what, I don't know. We took part in loading them on to the trucks of the Army of Yugoslavia; and in the transport to Pristina or behind Pristina, there's this power-plant called Obilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I didn't understand that answer. You said "one more time." Did you see this happen on another occasion as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I didn't see that happening, that they would wear these uniforms, put them on, and be killed; but another time I saw a group who were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, on this occasion where you did see what happened, was Zemunac the only person to shoot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. He used this machine-gun that we called Ceca then. He did the shooting. Now, was it anybody else? No. I just know that he did the shooting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were there other VJ soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, there were others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was there anyone there who was in a superior position to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably. Just like we always had our own commander there, he probably had a commander, a komandir, above him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, my question to you is: Did you see any commanding officer there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not personally. It's not that I saw someone like that, but he was probably there among them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I recognise it's two minutes to 4.00. Do you want me to move on to another topic, or would you like to stop here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was going to say it's amazing what you can do in two minutes, but that will be enough for today I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We need to go into closed session for the witness to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 25th day of January, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.00 p.m.,
